## Results

### Data summary

After quality control filtering, 12,163 valid observation-days across
35 calendar years (1986--2025) were available for analysis. The
overall circular mean peak hour was 15:58:00 local time
(circular SD = 2.84 h), confirming that the daily maximum at
Épinal typically occurs in the mid-afternoon, consistent with
boundary-layer heating dynamics.

### Year--season interaction test

I first tested whether the year-slope differs across meteorological
seasons using a likelihood-ratio (LR) test comparing nested von Mises
GLMs (Methods). The interaction was significant ($\chi^2 = 13.71$,
df = 3, $p = 0.0033$), rejecting the null hypothesis that all four
seasons share a common trend. This result justifies examining seasonal
estimates as the primary framework rather than a single pooled
estimate.

### Primary analysis: seasonal stratification

Since the interaction test supports seasonal heterogeneity, I report
per-season von Mises regression estimates as the primary analysis.

**Winter (DJF)** shows a significant advance of $-0.189$ h/decade
(95\% bootstrap CI: $-0.342$, $-0.026$), corresponding to approximately
$-11$ min/decade. This is the only season whose slope survives
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at $\alpha = 0.05$ (Wald
$p = 0.0015$).

**Autumn (SON)** exhibits a moderate delay of $+0.085$ h/decade
($+5$ min/decade, 95\% CI: $-0.018$, $+0.189$), although the Wald
$p = 0.10$ does not survive FDR correction.

**Spring (MAM)** shows an advance of $-0.065$ h/decade ($-4$ min/decade,
95\% CI: $-0.145$, $+0.027$, Wald $p = 0.17$) and **summer (JJA)** a
near-zero shift of $+0.020$ h/decade ($+1$ min/decade, 95\% CI:
$-0.081$, $+0.118$, Wald $p = 0.68$), neither reaching significance.

| Season | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95\% bootstrap CI | Wald $p$ | BH rejected |
|--------|--------------------:|:-----------------:|:--------:|:-----------:|
| Winter (DJF) | $-0.1886$ | $(-0.342, -0.026)$ | $0.0015$ | Yes |
| Spring (MAM) | $-0.0650$ | $(-0.145, +0.027)$ | $0.17$ | No |
| Autumn (SON) | $+0.0850$ | $(-0.018, +0.189)$ | $0.10$ | No |
| Summer (JJA) | $+0.0195$ | $(-0.081, +0.118)$ | $0.68$ | No |

: Per-season slope estimates from the year--season interaction von
Mises GLM. Wald $p$-values are corrected via the Benjamini-Hochberg
procedure ($\alpha = 0.05$, $m = 4$). {#tbl-seasonal-primary}

Figure~\ref{fig-seasonal} presents the per-season trend panels.

![Seasonal von Mises regression trends. Each panel shows hexbin density
  of daily peak hours and the fitted trend line with 95% CI band.
  ](../results/figures/seasonal_trend.pdf){#fig-seasonal}

### Seasonal sensitivity analysis

Each season's trend estimate was tested across six methodological
variants (alternative tie-breaking, subsampling, amplitude thresholds)
to assess robustness. For winter, the significant advance is
consistently negative across all variants (range: $-0.14$ to
$-0.24$ h/decade), confirming it is not an artefact of parameter
choice. Autumn's positive slope, while non-significant, is directionally
consistent across variants. Spring and summer remain near zero
regardless of variant (full results in Table~S1).

### Supplementary: pooled trend estimate

For comparison with previous studies that report only annual-scale
estimates, I also fit the von Mises GLM to all observations pooled
across seasons. The pooled slope is $-0.0281$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap
CI: $-0.0699$, $0.0121$), corresponding to approximately $-1.7$ min/decade
with a 95% confidence interval spanning $-4.2$ to $+0.7$ min/decade.

This near-zero pooled estimate masks the opposing winter (negative) and
autumn (positive) trends, which cancel when aggregated --- a classic
Simpson's paradox. The pooled result should therefore be interpreted as
the annual average of heterogeneous seasonal signals rather than as the
primary finding.

Figure~\ref{fig-wrapped-scatter} shows the daily peak-hour observations
with the fitted pooled trend line and 95% confidence band. The
hexagonal binning reveals the dominant concentration of peak hours in
the 14:00--18:00 window (approximately $68.7\%$ of observations).

![Daily peak-hour observations (hexbin density) with von Mises
  regression trend line and 95% bootstrap confidence band.
  The circular y-axis (0h$\leftrightarrow$24h) is shown zoomed to
  8--22h for readability.](../results/figures/wrapped_scatter.pdf){#fig-wrapped-scatter}

### Pooled sensitivity analysis

All six pooled sensitivity variants produced results consistent with the
pooled estimate (Table~\ref{tbl-sensitivity}), confirming that the
near-zero annual average is not driven by any single methodological
choice.

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95% CI | n obs |
|---------|--------------------|----------|-------|
| Primary tie (earliest) | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| Latest tie | $-0.0358$ | $(-0.0784, 0.0054)$ | 12,163 |
| Min years = 20 | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| 3-hour subsampling | $-0.0225$ | $(-0.0680, 0.0199)$ | 12,163 |
| 6-hour subsampling | $-0.0536$ | $(-0.1117, 0.0023)$ | 12,163 |
| Min amplitude 1.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.0281$ | $(-0.0699, 0.0121)$ | 12,163 |
| Min amplitude 3.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.0177$ | $(-0.0592, 0.0241)$ | 11,457 |

: Pooled sensitivity analysis. CI bounds are 2.5th and 97.5th bootstrap
percentiles. {#tbl-sensitivity}

### Supplementary analyses

Temperature-weighted von Mises regression (weighting each day by its
diurnal amplitude) produced an estimate of $+0.0210$ h/decade
(95\% CI: $-0.0125$ to $+0.0528$), consistent with the pooled result.
The circular--linear rank correlation (Mardia 1976) yielded
$\rho_c = 0.025$ ($p = 0.021$), suggesting a very weak but statistically
detectable association.
